implementation_notes: C++11 gives the pattern two standard-library shapes: std::future<T>::wait_for(duration) returns future_status::timeout when the result is not ready (it may block longer than requested under scheduling pressure, and returns immediately for a deferred task), while std::condition_variable::wait_for(lock, duration, pred) reports cv_status::timeout or false for waits on shared state. Neither cancels the producer: the task behind the future keeps running in its thread, and the condition wait only stops the waiter, so the timeout has to be paired with a stop flag (or C++20 stop_token) when the work itself should stop.
pitfalls: wait_for may block longer than the requested duration (scheduling, resource contention) and returns immediately for a task launched with std::launch::deferred, so the elapsed time is never exactly the budget.
wait_for does not cancel the task: the std::async thread keeps running, so the work needs its own budget or a cooperative stop.
A std::future returned by std::async blocks in its destructor until the task completes, so abandoning it 'after the timeout' can still hang the caller at scope exit.

variants.name: C++20 jthread + stop_token cooperative cancellation
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 supplies the half the pattern was missing: a std::jthread owns a std::stop_source and hands its std::stop_token to the worker, and the condition_variable_any wait_for/wait_until overloads take that token so a stop request interrupts the timed wait instead of hiding inside it. std::stop_callback registers the action to run on the stop request (closing a socket, setting a flag), and the jthread destructor requests stop and joins, so a timeout path cannot leave a detached worker behind.
pitfalls: The stop_token must reach the blocking primitive: a wait on a plain std::condition_variable ignores request_stop and keeps blocking for the full duration.
request_stop does not interrupt a blocking syscall (read, recv); a stop_callback must close the descriptor, or the worker must tear the socket down itself.
request_stop only sets the flag - code that never checks stop_requested()/the token keeps running, so the timeout still is not a guarantee.

variants.name: Boost.Asio steady_timer deadline around an async operation
variants.implementation_notes: In asynchronous C++ the deadline is a second outstanding operation: a boost::asio::steady_timer with expires_after(duration) runs an async_wait whose handler cancels the real operation (socket.cancel()/close()) when it fires, while the operation's own handler calls timer.cancel() when it finishes first. Timer expiry and cancellation stay distinguishable because a cancelled wait handler is invoked with error_code == boost::asio::error::operation_aborted, and re-arming expires_after on an active timer cancels the pending wait, so the race is decided by the return value of expires_after.
pitfalls: Cancelling an Asio operation completes its handler with operation_aborted on the same thread: the timeout path and the normal path must agree who owns the buffer and the socket, or a cancelled handler frees state the other one still uses.
One timer per operation - sharing a steady_timer between concurrent operations makes the second expires_after cancel the first wait.
steady_timer is the right typedef because it uses the steady clock; system_timer follows the wall clock, so an adjustment can move the deadline.
